title: UAE Severs All Trade With Iran After Missiles Fall Near Its Coast; Hormuz Traffic Slows to Six Vessels as Oil Holds Above $91
subhead: The UAE formally halted all trade, financial and commercial ties with Iran after two ballistic missiles fell near its coast, a sharp break between two Gulf neighbors that deepens the region's economic fracture. Meanwhile Hormuz tanker traffic slid to six vessels on Tuesday and Brent held above $91 as both Washington and Tehran showed no appetite for talks.

sections.heading: UAE Freezes All Trade With Iran After Missiles Fall Near Its Coast
sections.body:
The United Arab Emirates has halted all trade, financial and commercial ties with Iran until further notice, after saying Tehran fired two ballistic missiles that fell near its territory, OilPrice.com reported Wednesday. The UAE Defense Ministry said late Tuesday that 'assessments revealed the two ballistic missiles detected, originating from Iran, were targeting maritime navigation and fell into the sea' — one outside the UAE's territorial waters and a second within them. Foreign Ministry strategic communications director Afra Al Hameli said the freeze was imposed 'in light of regional escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security.'

Iran denied the missiles originated from it. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei called the accusation 'baseless' and 'contrary to the principle of good neighbourliness,' warning regional countries against making 'baseless accusations' against Tehran, per the Times of Oman. The UAE is a major trade and re-export hub for Iran, and the freeze marks the first time a Gulf state has formally severed economic ties with Tehran during the war.
sections.whyItMatters: The UAE has been one of the Gulf's most pragmatic traders with Iran, and its decision to sever all economic ties is a qualitative break — not just a security posture but a commercial rupture. It removes a key channel for Iranian trade and re-exports, and signals that even the most commercially flexible Gulf states are now drawing a hard line against Tehran as the Hormuz standoff drags on.

sections.heading: Hormuz Traffic Slows to Six Vessels; Oil Rises for a Fourth Day
sections.body:
Commodity vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed further on Tuesday, with ship-tracking data from Kpler showing just six commodity vessels transiting the waterway, down from nine on Monday and below the 10-day average of 11, Reuters reported. One empty crude supertanker and two smaller tankers moved into the Gulf via a lane close to Oman, while two medium-range fuel tankers and a post-Panamax vessel transited outbound. The slowdown followed a cargo vessel being struck by an 'unknown projectile' during an outbound transit, per the UK Maritime Trade Operations.

Crude prices extended gains for a fourth day, with Brent trading at $91.53 a barrel and WTI at $85.47 on Wednesday, as both Iran and the United States showed no willingness to return to the negotiating table, OilPrice.com reported. The US insists the strait remains open while Iran maintains it is closed. Sparta Commodities senior oil analyst June Goh told Reuters that 'shipping risks are increasing again as attacks from Iran and Houthis remain prevalent in both key chokepoints,' though she noted Gulf producers are finding alternative export routes to the Gulf of Oman.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is now pricing a prolonged closure rather than a reversible shock. With transit volumes near a tenth of normal and both sides refusing talks, the question has shifted from when Hormuz reopens to how long the world absorbs the disruption — and whether alternative export routes out of the Gulf of Oman can meaningfully offset the shortfall.

sections.heading: Saudi Aramco Reroutes September Barrels to Europe via Egypt and Malta
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco will supply full contractual crude volumes to at least three European refiners in September, offering deliveries from Egypt, Saudi Arabia and through ship-to-ship transfers off Malta as the war disrupts the kingdom's normal export routes, Bloomberg reported via The Edge Malaysia. Two European refiners will take barrels from Egypt's Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, while a third can choose between Sidi Kerir, Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu or a ship-to-ship transfer off Malta. Aramco notified its European customers about a week later than usual.

The move follows Aramco resuming loadings at Ras Tanura and Juaymah last week after a three-week interruption, with three VLCCs loading roughly 2 million barrels each between August 12 and 16. The kingdom has increasingly diverted crude north through Egypt to Sidi Kerir as an alternative to sending tankers south from Yanbu through the Houthi-threatened Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Aramco is having a harder time placing September barrels with some Asian customers, who are pushing back against loading at Yanbu because of the Houthi threat.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is actively re-engineering its export logistics around two blocked chokepoints — Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb — by routing crude through Egypt and using ship-to-ship transfers. The shift shows how Gulf producers are adapting to a world where neither of their traditional maritime routes is reliable, and it gives European refiners supply certainty at a time of acute scarcity.

sections.heading: Murban Crude Jumps to 4-Month High as ADNOC Cuts Asia Supply
sections.body:
The price of Murban crude, the UAE's flagship grade, surged to a four-month high this week, trading at a nearly $7 per barrel premium over Brent at $97.75, after reports that ADNOC will cut its crude allocations for August and September for some customers, OilPrice.com reported. ADNOC plans to reduce by about 5% the supply it is offering in spot tenders to Asian buyers this month and next, according to anonymous sources cited by Bloomberg, with the lower supply resulting from maintenance on some of ADNOC's onshore fields in Abu Dhabi.

The premium is the highest Murban has held over Brent since early April, when supply constraints from the Middle East peaked with the closed Strait of Hormuz. Since June, ADNOC has sold an estimated more than 100 million barrels in spot tenders as the Gulf producer that left OPEC on May 1 pushes to sell increased volumes internationally. The UAE has kept its oil flowing by shuttling crude through the chokepoint, using its onshore pipeline to bypass Hormuz, and shipping tankers through the strait in dark mode.
sections.whyItMatters: ADNOC's decision to trim spot supply to Asia — even as it expands overall exports — shows the UAE is prioritizing premium pricing over volume in a tight market. The Murban premium is a direct signal of how scarce Gulf crude has become for Asian buyers, and it underscores the UAE's post-OPEC strategy of maximizing value from its flexible export network.

sections.heading: Iraq-Syria Pipeline to Bypass Hormuz Is 4 Years and $15 Billion Away
sections.body:
The project to ship Iraqi crude to Syria's Mediterranean coast to bypass the Strait of Hormuz is still at least four years and $15 billion in investments away, sources familiar with the project told Reuters. The pipeline plan, supported by the US administration as a way to reduce the importance of Hormuz in global oil supply, is being reviewed by a consortium that includes US supermajor Chevron. The US is touting the project as making Hormuz 'irrelevant' within two years, but the actual construction would need at least four years, the sources said.

The existing pipeline that hasn't been operational in more than two decades cannot be used for the new project, which will need new infrastructure — complicating the plan, raising costs and extending the timeline. Still, the Hormuz crisis that cut off most of Iraq's crude exports has accelerated plans by Iraq and Syria to rebuild the damaged Kirkuk-to-Baniyas route. Youssef Qablawi, CEO of state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, said the renovation of the pipeline from Haditha in Iraq to the Syrian port of Baniyas would take 'three years at most,' with a capacity of between 1.5 million and 2 million barrels per day.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Washington's two-year promise and the four-year-plus reality highlights how far the region is from a genuine Hormuz alternative. The pipeline would be crucial for Iraq's exports, Syria's post-war economy and reducing Iranian leverage over the strait — but it is a long-term bet, not a near-term fix, and its feasibility depends on security and investment that remain uncertain.

sections.heading: UK Energy Bills to Hit 3-Year High; India Pivots to Piped Gas
sections.body:
UK household energy bills are set to rise a further 4% from October to their highest level since the summer of 2023, as the Iran war tightens global gas supply, consultancy Cornwall Insight said Wednesday. The energy regulator Ofgem is expected to raise the price cap to £1,729 ($2,344) for the October-December period, up from the current £1,663. The projected increase is 'being driven by ongoing uncertainty over the US-Iran conflict, with wholesale prices for the coming winter having risen to their highest level in almost four years,' Cornwall Insight said. UK inflation rose to 2.9% in July, the highest in four months, per BBC data.

In India, the government approved an Incentive Scheme for Promotion of Domestic PNG Connections, effective September 1, to fast-track piped natural gas connections as the cost of importing LPG has soared since the war choked off supply from the Middle East. Around 60% of Indian households rely on LPG for primary cooking fuel, and 90% of all Indian LPG imports passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war. Under the scheme, eligible city gas distributors get an additional 200 standard cubic meters of domestically-produced, lower-priced gas for every incremental domestic PNG connection.
sections.whyItMatters: The war's cost is now hitting household budgets directly — UK bills at a three-year high and inflation rebounding, while India scrambles to shift households off imported LPG onto domestic piped gas. These are the political and social consequences of the Hormuz closure that will shape how long governments can tolerate the disruption before pushing harder for a diplomatic resolution.

sections.heading: Russia's Refining Crisis Deepens: Ufa Fire, Diesel Exports Crash
sections.body:
Ukraine hit a refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan region overnight in a drone attack that sparked a fire, as Kyiv continues to pound Russian energy infrastructure, OilPrice.com reported. One of the refineries in Ufa caught fire, the region's governor Radiy Khabirov said, with repairs expected within a few days. Ufa and the surrounding area host three refineries, all owned and operated by Bashneft, a unit of Russia's biggest oil company Rosneft.

Russia's diesel and gasoil exports crashed in the first seven days of August to just 80,000 barrels per day, the lowest in many years, as Moscow extended restrictions on diesel exports amid a fuel crisis triggered by Ukrainian attacks on refineries. Russia has been suffering from gasoline and diesel shortages for over three months, as Ukraine's drone campaign forced many large processing sites offline in the spring and summer. Last week, Ukraine also attacked Ust-Luga, the top Russian port for exports of oil and other commodities from the Baltic Sea.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's sustained drone campaign against Russian refining is now visibly constraining Russia's export capacity — diesel exports at multi-year lows even as global markets are tight. The Ufa strike shows the campaign is reaching deeper into Russia's refining heartland, compounding the fuel shortages that have already forced Moscow to import gasoline by sea from Asia.

bottomLine: The UAE's decision to sever all trade with Iran after missiles fell near its coast is the sharpest break yet between a Gulf state and Tehran — removing a key commercial channel and signaling that even the most pragmatic Gulf traders are now drawing a hard line. Hormuz traffic slid to six vessels on Tuesday and oil held above $91 as both Washington and Tehran showed no appetite for talks, while Saudi Arabia rerouted September barrels to Europe via Egypt and Malta and ADNOC's Murban grade hit a four-month high on reduced Asia supply. The Iraq-Syria pipeline touted as a Hormuz alternative remains four years and $15 billion away, and the war's cost is now hitting households directly — UK bills at a three-year high, India shifting off imported LPG, and Russia's refining crisis deepening with diesel exports at multi-year lows. The region is consolidating into hardened blocs, and the near-term question is whether any diplomatic path survives the UAE's rupture with Tehran.
sources: OilPrice.com, Reuters, Bloomberg, The Edge Malaysia, Kpler, UK Maritime Trade Operations, Sparta Commodities, ING, Times of Oman, UAE Defense Ministry, UAE Foreign Ministry, Cornwall Insight, BBC, Government of India, ICIJ, CNN
